summary: Round 2's fixes land as described. The forced test now covers the whole `needCommits` list, so a named fix that a reshape forces is no longer demanded. An out-of-range named disposition is refused at intake. A stray entry beside a named call is warned in its own words. The prompt and the agent file both ask for a task of its own per stated fix. What remains is mostly wording and edge reads around those fixes: the intake check is stricter than the field's readers (R3-1), and the override warning still says 'changed away from defer' for overrides that never were deferrals (R3-5). One could-not-confirm item asks whether a resume clears the new resolve-time stops, since the resume line says the person fixed the cause by hand (R3-4). The repository has no scheduled or queued work, so no overlap applies.

findings.title: The intake check refuses a null or empty disposition, which every reader of the field takes as none
findings.description: R2-6's intake loop (lines 180-184) fails the launch for any `disposition` that is not `undefined` and not one of `CALL_ENDS`, so `disposition: ''` and `disposition: null` now stop the run with `args.decisions must give a disposition of fix | defer | accept` before any agent runs. Every reader of the field tests it for truthiness: `overridesFor` (3733), the first-stop draft filter (3696), `effectiveDispositions` (3908), `asked` (3801) and `named` (3851). Before this change such a decision ran as a call with no disposition. The conditions it needs: a session writing an empty or null disposition. No documented path does. The skill records a disposition only as fix, defer or accept (SKILL.md lines 189, 215, 224, 228). The one place the workflow itself emits `|| ''` (the `overridesUnresolved` handoff, line 4857) lists only overrides, which always carry a disposition. The result is a loud refusal, not a silent misread.
findings.proposedFix: Either test `entry.disposition !== undefined && entry.disposition !== null && entry.disposition !== ''` before the enum check, so the intake reads absence the way the readers do, or keep the strict check and say in the comment above it that an empty value is refused on purpose.

findings.title: relaunch.how gives the plan dial's asks the changed-disposition shape, with a disposition key the skill never records for an ask
findings.description: `relaunch.how` says a plan-dial relaunch passes 'decisions for every ask and every changed disposition ({"choice", "notes", "date", "disposition": "fix|defer|accept"})'. Read literally, the shape with `disposition` covers both. The skill records an ask the way the decisions hand-off does, with no disposition (SKILL.md line 186), and gives the disposition only to a changed one (line 189). The sentence is unchanged from main (line 2620 there). This pull request is what makes the difference matter. Since #99 a call whose decision carries a disposition is a named call: it is asked for no statement (`asked`, line 3801, and the prompt's `anyNamed` sentence), and it is held to what it names (`namedUnplanned`/`namedPlanned`, lines 3889-3896). So a session that followed `relaunch.how` and put a disposition it guessed on an ask would have that guess decide the call. For example, 'Keep it, add a comment' guessed as `accept` stops at resolve on its comment task. Whether a session reads `relaunch.how` over the skill is session behaviour; what is verified is that the two texts disagree.
findings.proposedFix: Split the plan clause of `relaunch.how`: 'decisions for every ask ({"choice", "notes", "date"}) and every changed disposition ({"choice", "notes", "date", "disposition": "fix|defer|accept"})'.

findings.title: Out-of-range statements are filtered before firstPerId, so a valid second statement is kept silently
findings.description: Line 3797 runs `firstPerId(...)` over `(out.decided || []).filter((item) => CALL_ENDS.includes(item.disposition))`. A first statement outside the three is dropped before the repeat check sees it. So `[{id: 'R1-1', disposition: 'mitigate'}, {id: 'R1-1', disposition: 'fix'}]` keeps `fix` with no 'more than once' warning. The comment at 3788-3789 says 'the first it returned, and a value outside the three is no statement'. The code keeps the first valid one instead. The conditions it needs: `RESOLVE_SCHEMA` gives `decided[].disposition` an enum of `CALL_ENDS` (line 905), so in the agent's own run the harness refuses such a value. A result has to bypass that schema to reach here. This is distinct from R1-4 (the warning firing for identical repeats) and R1-6 (the message for an out-of-range value), both declined: it is about the order of the two steps.
findings.proposedFix: Run `firstPerId` over `out.decided || []` first and then drop a kept entry whose disposition is outside `CALL_ENDS`. Or keep the order and reword the comment to say the first valid statement is kept.

findings.title: The new resolve-time stops rely on a resume whose line tells the resolve agent the person fixed the cause and the earlier files stand
findings.description: This pull request adds six stops at stage `resolve`: unstated (3804), undeferred (3876), unplanned (3880), planned (3884), namedUnplanned (3891) and namedPlanned (3895). Each is caused by the resolve agent's own output, not by anything the person can fix. `docs/running.md` (line 126) says each one resumes 'at the resolve step that ran ..., where the resolve agent runs again'. The rerun's prompt gets `resumeLine` (line 575, unchanged by this pull request). It says 'the person has since fixed the cause by hand' and 'What an earlier attempt already made stands (a written file)'. It does carry the error text. The agent file's steps 2 and 3 act on *pending* Decisions entries and `Pending decision` tasks, and on a rerun the first attempt has already decided both. The shaper gets a 'rewrite from scratch' sentence on resume (line 567); the resolve agent gets nothing like it. What I tried: I read `resumeLine`, `run()` (589-594), the agent file and the docs. Whether a rerun reads the error and corrects `plan.md`, or returns the same tasks and repeats the stop, is model behaviour the repository and the scripted loop test cannot show. The person can always restate the answer instead, which changes the prompt. The same mechanism already served the `unentered` stop (#97, R2-13) before this pull request.
findings.proposedFix: Give the resolve agent a resume sentence like the shaper's: when the label is a resolve's, add that the earlier attempt's plan was refused for the reason given and that it should revisit the decided entries and tasks it wrote, not only pending ones. Or have docs/running.md tell the person to restate the answer, or correct plan.md, before resuming.
findings.wouldConfirm: A guided run that stops at `resolve r1` with an accept stated beside a task with files, then resumes unchanged, showing whether the rerun returns the same task and stops again.

findings.title: The new comment says an override is a finding changed away from defer, and the override warning still says so for a decline overruled to fix
findings.description: R2-3's fix added the comment 'An override is a finding the person changed away from defer' (3820-3822). It also kept the override warning at 3827, 'a finding the person changed away from defer'. `overridesFor` (3733) takes any in-scope finding whose decision carries a disposition and that is not a call. `awayFromDefer` (3739) is true for any disposition other than `defer`. So an override from decline to fix, or from fix to accept, both of which the skill offers (SKILL.md lines 189 and 215), passes `awayFromDefer`. A stray resolve entry beside one is warned as 'a finding the person changed away from defer', though the shaper never deferred it. The warning's wording comes from main (line 3767 there, #103 R2-8). The comment that states the premise as fact is in round 2's fix diff. R2-3 fixed this wording for a call whose decision names a fix; this is the same wording on overrides, which that fix left as it was.
findings.proposedFix: Reword the comment to 'An override is a finding whose disposition the person changed', and the warning to '... a finding whose disposition the person changed to <disposition>; the entry is dropped, since the decision stands', using `roundDecisions[id].disposition` as the named-call warning does.

findings.title: resolveWith tells a call from an override two ways: strayNamed reads `calls`, whose() reads `newOverrides`
findings.description: `strayNamed` (3824, added by R2-3's fix) tests `calls.some((call) => call.id === id)`. `whose` (3853) tests `newOverrides.some((f) => f.id === id)`. Both decide whether a decision is a call or an override, and the wording of the stray warnings and the named-check stops depends on that answer. I traced both resolve paths (3959 with `calls, overrides`; 4030 with `raised, []` after `calls = calls.concat(raised)`). The two agree today: `overridesFor` excludes every known call, and a raised call's resolve passes no overrides. So this is a maintenance cost, not a wrong message: two predicates that must stay in agreement.
findings.proposedFix: Define one local predicate in resolveWith, e.g. `const isCall = (id) => calls.some((call) => call.id === id)`, and use it in both `strayNamed` and `whose`.

accounting.ref: Claims main's removed `accepted` set left a stated-fix call undemanded after a reshape re-sorts it to accept. On main, `accepted` was read from finalDispositions (main line 3969). For a call, that is the shaper's disposition, and the shape schema allows only fix, decline, defer, ask (round) or fix, ask, none (human), line 885, so a reshape cannot produce `accept` and main demanded the call's resolve task too. The pull request keeps a stated fix demanded whatever a reshape does on purpose. A reshape rewriting a decided finding's task is #106's subject.

list.summary: The stated-fix branch of needCommits now demands a commit for a call even after a reshape re-sorts it to accept. Before #99 the removed `accepted` set left it undemanded, and the plan the implementer builds no longer holds the task.
list.failure_scenario: Guided run. R1-1 is answered 'Change it', and the resolve states fix with a task in app/x.php. The plan approver bounces, and the reshape (against its prompt) re-sorts R1-1 to accept and rewrites its task to 'Accepted, no change'. effectiveDispositions shows R1-1 as accept to the plan approver and the implementer, so nothing is built for it. needCommits still demands R1-1 through `stated`. The judge fails with 'no commit names R1-1', and the repair is told to commit for a finding the plan shows as accepted. The round then stops at check, a stop that resumes at the build and cannot replan, which is the stop the PR's own resolve-time checks exist to prevent. On main, `accepted.has('R1-1')` left it out. Spec decision 16 covers only the opposite case (accept re-sorted to fix). Related to #106 (a reshape changing a decided finding's task), which does not cover a decided fix.

list.summary: The new resolve-time stops (unstated, stated defer/fix/accept against the plan, named fix/accept) all rely on a resume rerunning the resolve agent. The resume line tells that agent the person fixed the cause by hand and that the earlier attempt's files stand.
list.failure_scenario: The resolve states accept for R1-1 beside a task with files and the round stops at `resolve r1`. The person relaunches with resume and fixes nothing, since the cause is the agent's own inconsistent output. resumeLine (line 575) says 'the person has since fixed the cause by hand ... What an earlier attempt already made stands (a written file)'. The rerun finds shape.md already decided (nothing pending) and plan.md still holding the task with files, so it is told to keep it and can return the same tasks, and the same stop repeats. docs/running.md promises 'where the resolve agent runs again' as if that clears the stop. The mechanism existed before for `unentered`, but this PR adds six stop kinds that depend on it.

list.summary: relaunch.how tells the session that a plan-dial relaunch passes 'decisions for every ask and every changed disposition ({choice, notes, date, disposition})'. Since #99 an ask whose decision carries a disposition is a named call: the resolve agent is never asked for a statement, and the disposition is whatever the session guessed.
list.failure_scenario: On the plan dial the person picks 'Keep it, add a comment' for ask R1-2. A session following relaunch.how literally adds a disposition and infers 'accept'. resolveWith then skips R1-2 from `asked`, the prompt says it has no entry in decided, and namedPlanned stops the run at resolve because the comment task has files. The person can only restate the answer, and the same relaunch replays the same refusal. This is the session-side inference #99 set out to remove. The skill's own plan-dial text records an ask without a disposition, so the two documents disagree on the key that now decides how a call is read.

list.summary: firstPerId runs after statements outside fix, defer and accept are dropped. When the first statement for an id is invalid and a later one is valid, the later one is kept with no 'more than once' warning, though the comment says the first statement returned is kept.
list.failure_scenario: The resolve returns decided [{id:'R1-1', disposition:'mitigate'}, {id:'R1-1', disposition:'fix'}], for example where the harness's schema check is not applied, such as a replayed result. The filter drops 'mitigate', firstPerId sees one entry, and 'fix' is taken silently. A fix is then demanded and any deferred entry is dropped, with no warning that the agent stated two different things for R1-1. Filtering after firstPerId would make the first statement count, as the comment and the stage error say. This sits next to the declined R1-4 and R1-6 but is not either of them: it is about the order of the two steps.

list.summary: The new intake check (R2-6) refuses any `disposition` that is not undefined and not one of the three values, so null or an empty string now fail the launch. Every reader of the field (overridesFor, the first-stop draft filter, effectiveDispositions, isDeferral, `asked`, `named`) treats a falsy disposition as none.
list.failure_scenario: A relaunch whose args.decisions carries {'R1-1': {choice:'Keep it', notes:'...', date:'...', disposition:''}} or disposition:null, for example a session copying the empty `disposition` field the overridesUnresolved handoff returns (line 4857, `|| ''`). Before this change it ran as a call with no disposition. Now it hard-fails with 'args.decisions must give a disposition of fix | defer | accept' before any agent runs. The check is stricter than every reader, so a value the workflow would have read correctly is refused.

list.summary: The new comment says 'An override is a finding the person changed away from defer', but overridesFor takes any finding with a decision disposition. The strayChanged warning (line 3827) therefore still claims 'changed away from defer' for a decline overruled to fix and for a fix changed to accept, neither of which was ever a deferral.
list.failure_scenario: Plan dial: the person overrules decline R1-3 to fix, and the resolve agent also returns a stray deferred entry for R1-3. awayFromDefer is true, R1-3 is not a call, and the warning reads 'the resolve agent listed R1-3 as deferred, a finding the person changed away from defer'. The shaper declined it and never deferred it, which is the wrong-history wording R2-3 fixed for named calls only. The comment R2-3 added states the false premise as fact.

list.summary: resolveWith decides 'call or override' two ways for the same fact: strayNamed tests `calls.some(...)`, while `whose()` at line 3853 tests `newOverrides.some(...)`.
list.failure_scenario: Cost: two predicates that must stay in agreement, in a function where the wording of every stray and named-check message depends on that fact. A later change to how overrides or raised calls are collected (the reshape path already resolves an override's finding a second time as a raised call) can make the warnings and the stop messages disagree about whose decision it is. One local predicate, used by both, does the same job.
